text: Every ship that left the port paid a penny a ton toward the light. Every ship that came back paid it again. The owners of the ships that never came back were the ones who complained that it wasn't bright enough.
strengths: the repeated opening sounds like the toll book it describes
the third sentence breaks the pattern to deliver the point
the humour is dry and grim
weaknesses: two matched openings make the construction audible
a speech device that tips into oratory if used again
spokenRhythm: Two mirrored sentences set up a pattern, and a longer third sentence breaks it.
narrativeFunction: Explains how a lighthouse was funded and who had reason to doubt it.
whyItWorks: Repetition with a break is one of the oldest spoken patterns, and here it suits the subject, because tolls are repetitive. The listener expects a third Every ship and instead hears the owners who lost theirs, which makes the dry point land.
whyItFails: Matched openings are a rhetorical device the ear notices. Once in a film it sounds like a person making a point. Twice and it sounds like a sermon, and a writing model that learns it will reach for it whenever it wants emphasis. Keep it only where the subject is itself repetitive, and never in the same sequence as another patterned passage.
rewrite: Every ship paid a penny a ton toward the light, once on the way out and again on the way home. The owners of the ships that never came home were the ones who complained that it wasn't bright enough.

text: The bank opened at nine. By ten there was a queue. By noon there was no money left.
strengths: each sentence is complete, with a subject and a verb
a whole morning in eighteen words
weaknesses: three very short sentences in a row sit right on the edge of a fragment run
the matching openings make the device visible
spokenRhythm: Three short beats that each move the clock forward, with no long sentence to release them.
narrativeFunction: Compresses a run on a bank into a single morning.
whyItWorks: Used once at the climax of a sequence, a run of short complete sentences can feel like the hours passing, and a time stamp in each one gives the escalation a real basis. It is clear, quick and concrete.
whyItFails: Three short sentences of almost the same length are the cadence of a trailer. Without a longer sentence to follow and resolve them, the passage ends on a drumbeat rather than a thought. If the film has already used a run of short sentences, this one should be rewritten, and it should never be followed by a one-word fragment.
rewrite: The bank opened at nine, and by ten there was a queue. By noon the money had run out.

text: The man who opened the coffee house — a former ship's purser who had never run so much as a market stall — chose the one street in the town that every merchant crossed twice a day.
strengths: the aside sets inexperience against a shrewd choice
a single pair of dashes, not a chain
the character is introduced through what he did
weaknesses: the listener has to hold the subject across a fourteen-word interruption
dashes give a voice no clear instruction
spokenRhythm: A sentence that starts, drops into a lower aside, and has to climb back to its verb.
narrativeFunction: Introduces the founder of a coffee house and the one decision that made it work.
whyItWorks: A good reader can make a single aside sound like natural speech, a slight drop of the voice before the point. The contrast between a man with no shop experience and a perfectly chosen street is genuinely dry.
whyItFails: On the page the dashes are tidy. Aloud, the main clause is suspended for so long that the verb arrives without its subject in mind, and a synthetic voice may read the dashes as a pause or ignore them. The habit of reaching for a dash instead of a second sentence is one of the clearest marks of machine prose, so a single aside is the limit, and two sentences are usually better.
rewrite: The man who opened the coffee house had been a ship's purser, and he had never run so much as a market stall. He chose the one street in the town that every merchant crossed twice a day.
